passages.A1X_TOM: Tom is twelve years old. He lives with his mother, his father and his little sister, Amy, in a small house in York. Tom's father is a bus driver and his mother works in a shop. Tom goes to school by bike, but Amy walks with her mother. After school Tom plays football in the park. He doesn't like computer games. In the evening the family eats dinner together at seven o'clock.
passages.A1X_SHOP: Corner Shop — Opening times. Monday to Friday: 7 am to 9 pm. Saturday: 8 am to 9 pm. Sunday: 10 am to 4 pm. We sell bread, milk, fruit, newspapers and stamps. Sorry, we do not take cards for payments under £5.
passages.A1X_EMAIL: Hi Lena, I'm in Brighton with my cousin Mark. The weather is sunny and warm. We go to the beach every morning. Mark can swim very well but I can't, so I sit on the sand and read. Yesterday we ate fish and chips. Tomorrow we want to visit the pier. See you on Friday! Love, Nina
passages.A1X_ROOM: My bedroom is small but I love it. There is a bed next to the window and a big desk under the shelves. My books are on the shelves and my guitar is behind the door. The walls are blue. There isn't a TV in my room, but there is a radio on the desk.
passages.A1X_DAY: Ali gets up at half past six. He has a shower and then he has breakfast: tea, bread and an egg. He catches the train at quarter past seven. He works in a hospital in Leeds. He finishes work at four o'clock. On Wednesdays he goes to an English class in the evening.
passages.A1X_NOTE: Dear Mum, I'm at Sara's house. We're doing our homework. Her dad can drive me home at eight o'clock. There's some pasta in the fridge for dinner. Please feed the cat! Love, Jess
passages.A1X_PARTY: Come to my birthday party! Saturday 14th June, 3 pm to 6 pm, at 22 Park Road. There is food and music. Please bring your swimming things because we have a pool. Please tell me by Wednesday if you can come. Call Ben: 07700 900123.
passages.A2X_JOB: Hannah started a new job last month at a garden centre near Bristol. Before that, she worked in an office for six years, but she was bored because she sat at a computer all day. Now she spends most of the day outside, helping customers to choose plants. The pay is lower than in her old job, so she cycles to work instead of driving to save money. She says she feels healthier and much happier. Next spring she is going to start a course in garden design.
passages.A2X_TRIP: Last summer my family went camping in the Lake District for a week. On the first night it rained so much that water came into our tent, and we had to sleep in the car. The next day the sun came out and we climbed a hill called Catbells. It wasn't very high, but the views were wonderful. My little brother was scared of the sheep at first, but by the end of the week he was feeding them. We're planning to go back next year, but this time we're going to stay in a cottage.
passages.A2X_ADVERT: FLAT TO RENT — Two bedrooms, first floor, five minutes' walk from the station. Fully furnished, with a new kitchen. Rent: £850 a month, plus bills. No pets. Available from 1st March. Students welcome. To arrange a visit, email Mr Patel (no phone calls after 8 pm).
passages.A2X_CLUB: Riverside Running Club meets every Tuesday and Thursday at 6.30 pm outside the sports centre. Beginners are welcome: on Tuesdays there is a slower group that runs 3 km. On Thursdays we run 8 km along the river. The first two sessions are free; after that membership costs £20 a year. Wear comfortable shoes and bring a bottle of water. We don't run if there is ice on the paths.
passages.A2X_MESSAGE: Hi Dan, sorry, I can't meet you at the cinema tonight. My boss asked me to stay late because a colleague is ill. Could we go on Saturday afternoon instead? The film is on at 2.15 and 5.30. I've already bought my ticket for tonight, but the cinema says I can change it for free. Let me know which time is better for you. Kate
passages.A2X_MUSEUM: The Science Museum in London is free to enter, but some special exhibitions cost money. It is open every day from 10 am to 6 pm, and on the last Wednesday of each month it stays open until 10 pm for adults only. The museum café on the ground floor is often busy at lunchtime, so visitors can also eat their own food in the picnic area in the basement.
passages.A2X_HOLIDAY: When I was a child, we never went abroad on holiday. Every August we drove to my grandparents' farm in Wales. My grandfather got up at five to milk the cows, and I sometimes helped him. In the evenings there was no television, so we played cards or listened to my grandmother's stories. At the time I wanted to go to Spain like my friends, but now those are my happiest memories.
passages.B1X_VOLUNTEER: When Priya retired from teaching, she expected to enjoy a quiet life in her garden. Within a month, however, she was bored. A neighbour suggested volunteering at the local library, which was struggling to stay open after the council cut its budget. Priya now runs a homework club for children three afternoons a week and has persuaded four former colleagues to join her. 'Some of the children don't have a quiet place to study at home,' she explains. 'Here they get help, and the library gets more visitors, which makes it harder for the council to close it.' Last year visitor numbers rose by a third.
passages.B1X_PHONES: A secondary school in Kent has banned mobile phones during the school day, and the head teacher says the results have been surprising. Students must leave their phones in lockers when they arrive and can collect them at 3.30. At first many parents complained that they would not be able to contact their children in an emergency, so the school agreed that parents could phone the office instead. Teachers report that students now talk to each other more at lunchtime and that there have been fewer arguments that start online. Not everyone agrees, though: some older students say they should be trusted to decide for themselves.
passages.B1X_REVIEW: I had high hopes for 'The Lighthouse', a new café on the seafront, because a friend had recommended it. The building is beautiful and the sea views are amazing, especially from the upstairs room. Unfortunately, the service didn't match the setting. We waited twenty-five minutes for two coffees, and when they arrived, one of them was cold. The cakes, on the other hand, were delicious and reasonably priced. I'd go back for the cakes and the view, but I'd avoid weekends, when it's clearly too busy for the staff to cope.
passages.B1X_COMMUTE: For ten years Martin drove forty minutes to his office in Leeds. When his company allowed staff to work from home three days a week, he thought he would save time and money. He did, but he also found that he was working longer hours, because there was no clear end to the day. He solved this by going for a walk at half past five every evening, 'pretending to come home from work'. He also joined a local choir to meet people, as he missed chatting to colleagues. Overall, he says, he would never go back to commuting every day.
passages.B1X_RECYCLE: From next month, households in the town will receive three bins instead of two. The green bin will be for garden waste, the blue bin for paper, cans and plastic bottles, and the black bin for everything else. Food waste must now go in a small brown container, which will be collected every week. Black bins will be emptied every two weeks rather than weekly. The council says the changes will save money and increase recycling, but some residents are worried that bins will smell in the summer.
passages.B1X_INTERVIEW: Interviewer: You started your bakery when you were only nineteen. Wasn't that risky? — Leah: Of course. I'd failed my exams and didn't know what to do, so my aunt let me use her kitchen at night. I sold bread at a market on Saturdays. — Interviewer: When did you realise it could be a real business? — Leah: When a café asked me to supply them every day. I couldn't do it alone, so I took a loan and rented a small shop. — Interviewer: Any advice for young people? — Leah: Don't wait until everything is perfect. Start small and learn from your mistakes.
passages.B1X_FESTIVAL: The Edinburgh Festival Fringe takes place every August and is often described as the largest arts festival in the world. Unlike many festivals, it has no selection committee: anyone with a venue can take part, which means that famous comedians perform alongside students putting on their first show. This openness is part of its charm, but it also means quality varies enormously. Many performers lose money, because venues are expensive and tickets for unknown shows can be hard to sell. Even so, people keep coming back, hoping to be discovered.
passages.B2X_SLEEP: Teenagers are often accused of being lazy when they stay in bed until midday at weekends. Yet sleep researchers argue that the problem is largely biological. During adolescence, the body releases the sleep hormone melatonin later in the evening, which means that many teenagers genuinely cannot fall asleep before eleven. Since school starts early, they build up a 'sleep debt' during the week and try to repay it at weekends. Some schools in the UK and the US have experimented with later start times, reporting better attendance and concentration. Critics point out, however, that later starts create problems for parents' working hours and for after-school activities.
passages.B2X_HIGHSTREET: Across Britain, high streets that once thrived are now lined with empty shops. Online shopping is the most obvious cause, but it is not the only one: high business rates, expensive parking and the growth of out-of-town shopping centres have all played a part. Some towns are fighting back by reinventing their centres as places to spend time rather than simply to buy things. Empty units have been turned into community spaces, small workshops and cafés, and markets have been revived. The towns that succeed, experts say, are those that offer an experience that cannot be downloaded.
passages.B2X_MEMORY: Most of us believe that our memories work like video recordings, faithfully storing what happened. Psychological research suggests otherwise. Each time we recall an event, we rebuild it, and in doing so we can unknowingly add details or change them. In one well-known experiment, participants who watched a film of a car accident gave higher estimates of the cars' speed when asked how fast they were going when they 'smashed' into each other than when the word 'hit' was used. A week later, those in the 'smashed' group were also more likely to remember seeing broken glass, although there had been none.
passages.B2X_REWILD: In parts of Scotland, landowners are 'rewilding' their estates: rather than managing the land for sheep or shooting, they allow forests to regenerate and reintroduce species that disappeared long ago. Supporters argue that rewilding increases biodiversity, stores carbon and can bring jobs through tourism. Opponents, many of them farmers, fear it threatens traditional ways of life and worry about the impact of predators on livestock. The debate is particularly heated over proposals to bring back the lynx, a wild cat that has been absent from Britain for over a thousand years.
passages.B2X_GIG: Freelance work arranged through apps — delivering food, driving taxis, doing small online tasks — is often praised for its flexibility. Workers can choose when to log on and can combine several jobs. But critics argue that this flexibility mostly benefits the companies. Because app workers are usually classed as self-employed, they are not entitled to holiday pay or sick pay, and their income can fall suddenly if the company changes how it pays. In 2021 the UK Supreme Court ruled that drivers for one large company should be treated as workers, with rights to the minimum wage and paid holidays.
passages.B2X_LANG: For years it was assumed that children who grow up speaking two languages would be confused and fall behind at school. More recent research has largely overturned this view. Bilingual children may initially have a smaller vocabulary in each language, but their total vocabulary is usually similar to that of monolingual children. Some studies have also suggested that switching between languages trains the brain to ignore distractions, although this claimed 'bilingual advantage' remains controversial, as several large studies have failed to find it.
passages.B2X_EMAILCOMPLAINT: Dear Customer Services, I am writing to complain about the washing machine I ordered from your website on 3 May. Although I paid extra for next-day delivery, it did not arrive until 9 May, and I had to take two days off work to wait for it. When it was finally installed, it leaked water across the kitchen floor during its first cycle. I would like you to collect the machine and either replace it or give me a full refund, including the delivery charge. I would also appreciate some compensation for the time I have lost. I look forward to hearing from you within seven days. Yours faithfully, R. Okafor
passages.C1X_NUDGE: Governments have increasingly turned to 'nudges' — small changes in how choices are presented — to influence behaviour without banning anything or raising prices. Making pension saving the default option, for instance, so that employees must actively opt out rather than opt in, has dramatically increased participation in the UK. Advocates describe this as 'libertarian paternalism': people remain free to choose, yet are steered towards decisions that serve their long-term interests. Critics, however, question who decides what those interests are, and warn that techniques which work precisely because people do not notice them sit uneasily with democratic transparency. Others argue that nudges are too modest to tackle problems such as obesity or climate change, and may serve as a convenient excuse for avoiding more effective but less popular regulation.
passages.C1X_TRANSLATION: Literary translators are frequently described as invisible, and the best translations are often praised for reading as though they had been written in the target language. Yet this ideal of seamlessness is itself contested. Some translators deliberately retain unfamiliar syntax or untranslated words, arguing that smoothing away every trace of the original amounts to a kind of cultural erasure, presenting foreign experience in comfortably domestic terms. Readers, they suggest, should be reminded that they are encountering another culture. Publishers, mindful of sales, tend to favour fluency, and translators' names still rarely appear on book covers, though campaigns in recent years have begun to change this.
passages.C1X_URBAN: The notion that cities are inherently bad for the environment has been challenged by urban economists. Per person, residents of dense cities typically consume less energy than suburban or rural dwellers: they live in smaller homes that share walls, travel shorter distances and are more likely to walk or use public transport. The difficulty is that density is frequently unpopular with existing residents, who object to taller buildings and fear congestion and the loss of green space. Planning systems that give considerable weight to local objections may therefore, paradoxically, push development outwards, generating precisely the car-dependent sprawl that environmental policy seeks to avoid.
passages.C1X_SCIENCE: The 'replication crisis' refers to the discovery that a surprisingly large proportion of published findings, particularly in psychology and medicine, could not be reproduced when other researchers repeated the experiments. Several factors have been blamed. Journals have historically preferred striking, positive results, giving researchers an incentive to analyse their data in many ways until something appears significant. Small sample sizes make chance findings more likely. In response, many journals now encourage 'pre-registration', in which scientists publicly state their hypotheses and methods before collecting data, making it harder to present an exploratory fishing expedition as a confirmed prediction.
passages.C1X_WORK: Proponents of the four-day working week argue that productivity, rather than hours, should be the measure of work. Trials in which employees kept their full salary while working 80 per cent of their previous hours have reported that output was largely maintained, while staff reported lower stress and fewer sick days. Sceptics caution against generalising from these results. The companies that volunteered were, they note, disproportionately office-based firms already inclined towards flexible working; it is far less obvious how the model would apply to hospitals, schools or shops, where a reduction in hours means either hiring additional staff or reducing the service provided.
passages.C1X_ARCHIVE: When the family of a minor Victorian novelist donated a trunk of letters to a provincial archive, few expected it to attract much attention. Yet the correspondence revealed that she had been in regular contact with several of the leading reformers of her day and had anonymously written pamphlets that were widely circulated at the time. Scholars now argue that her marginal status in literary histories owes less to the quality of her work than to the conventions of the period, which discouraged women from publishing political writing under their own names. The discovery has prompted a broader reassessment of which voices were preserved, and why.
passages.C2X_ATTENTION: It has become something of a commonplace to lament the decline of attention, as though our capacity for sustained concentration were a natural resource being depleted by smartphones. The historical record complicates this narrative. Each new medium, from the novel to the radio, was accused in its day of corrupting the young and fragmenting thought. This is not to dismiss present concerns as mere moral panic; the business models of many digital platforms are explicitly predicated on capturing and monetising attention, which was not true of the eighteenth-century novel. Yet framing the problem as one of individual willpower risks obscuring its structural character, and places the burden of resistance on users rather than on the design choices that shape their behaviour.
passages.C2X_HERITAGE: Debates over contested statues often founder on a false dichotomy between preserving history and erasing it. Monuments are not history itself but interpretations of it, erected at particular moments to convey particular values, and frequently tell us more about those who commissioned them than about those they depict. Removing a statue to a museum, where it can be contextualised, is arguably less an act of erasure than of reclassification. Conversely, insisting that every monument remain untouched presupposes that the judgements of one generation should bind all those that follow — a position that would seem odd if applied to any other public decision.
passages.C2X_EXPERTISE: Public trust in expertise is sometimes portrayed as having collapsed, but surveys suggest a more nuanced picture: confidence in scientists and doctors remains comparatively high, while trust in politicians and journalists is markedly lower. What appears to have eroded is less faith in knowledge per se than deference to institutions perceived as remote or self-serving. Experts who acknowledge uncertainty openly, paradoxically, may command more durable trust than those who project unwarranted certainty, since the latter are exposed when, as is inevitable in fast-moving situations, initial advice has to be revised.
passages.C2X_LANGUAGECHANGE: Complaints about the degeneration of English are almost as old as the language itself. Jonathan Swift lamented the introduction of abbreviations such as 'mob'; later commentators deplored 'reliable' as an ugly hybrid. What such complaints tend to overlook is that change is not decay but the normal condition of every living language, and that today's solecism is frequently tomorrow's standard usage. Linguists are not, however, indifferent to how language is used; their objection is to the conflation of prestige with correctness, whereby the habits of a particular social group are presented as the logical rules of the language.
passages.C2X_PHILANTHROPY: Large-scale philanthropy is often greeted with uncritical gratitude, yet it raises awkward questions for democratic societies. When a foundation endows a hospital wing or funds an educational reform, it exercises considerable influence over public priorities without being accountable to the electorate. Defenders contend that private donors can take risks that governments, wary of public criticism, cannot, and that some of the most successful public-health campaigns were initially privately funded. Sceptics counter that the tax relief attached to charitable giving means that the public effectively subsidises decisions in which it has no say.
passages.C2X_MAPS: Maps carry an aura of objectivity that belies the choices underpinning them. Every projection of a spherical earth onto a flat surface involves distortion; the familiar Mercator projection, devised for navigation, preserves angles at the expense of area, making regions near the poles appear far larger than they are. Such technical compromises acquire political overtones when maps are used to represent the relative importance of nations. Beyond projection, cartographers decide what to include, what to name and in which language, decisions that have at times been instrumental in asserting territorial claims.

items.explanation: 'Techniques which work precisely because people do not notice them sit uneasily with democratic transparency.'

items.prompt: What do some argue nudges may be used as?
items.answer: an excuse to avoid stronger regulation
items.explanation: 'May serve as a convenient excuse for avoiding more effective but less popular regulation.'

items.prompt: What does 'libertarian paternalism' mean in the text?
items.answer: guiding choices while leaving people free to choose
distractors: forcing people to act in their interest
items.explanation: 'People remain free to choose, yet are steered towards decisions that serve their long-term interests.'

items.prompt: Why do some translators keep unfamiliar words and syntax?
items.answer: to remind readers they are meeting another culture
distractors: to make the book easier to read
items.explanation: 'Readers... should be reminded that they are encountering another culture.'

items.prompt: What do these translators consider a form of 'cultural erasure'?
items.answer: smoothing away all traces of the original
items.explanation: 'Smoothing away every trace of the original amounts to a kind of cultural erasure.'

items.prompt: Why do publishers tend to favour fluent translations?
items.explanation: 'Publishers, mindful of sales, tend to favour fluency.'

items.prompt: What has recently begun to change?
items.answer: Translators' names are appearing on covers more often.
items.explanation: 'Translators' names still rarely appear on book covers, though campaigns... have begun to change this.'

items.prompt: Why do city residents typically use less energy per person?
items.answer: smaller homes, shorter journeys and more public transport
items.explanation: They 'live in smaller homes that share walls, travel shorter distances and are more likely to walk or use public transport.'

items.prompt: What paradox does the writer describe?
items.answer: Local objections can cause more car-dependent sprawl.
distractors: Dense cities use more energy than villages.
items.explanation: Giving weight to local objections 'may... push development outwards, generating... sprawl'.

items.prompt: Why is density often unpopular with existing residents?
items.answer: They fear taller buildings, congestion and lost green space.
items.explanation: 'Existing residents... object to taller buildings and fear congestion and the loss of green space.'

items.prompt: What does the writer imply about the idea that cities are bad for the environment?
distractors: It applies only to old cities.
items.explanation: The notion 'has been challenged' with evidence about energy use per person.

items.prompt: What is the 'replication crisis'?
items.answer: Many published results couldn't be reproduced.
items.explanation: 'A surprisingly large proportion of published findings... could not be reproduced.'

items.prompt: How did journals' preferences contribute to the problem?
items.explanation: 'Journals have historically preferred striking, positive results.'

items.prompt: What is the purpose of pre-registration?
items.answer: to make it harder to present exploration as prediction
items.explanation: It makes it 'harder to present an exploratory fishing expedition as a confirmed prediction.'

items.prompt: Why do small sample sizes matter?
items.answer: They make chance findings more likely.
distractors: They make results easy to reproduce.
items.explanation: 'Small sample sizes make chance findings more likely.'

items.prompt: What did four-day week trials report?
items.answer: Output was largely maintained and stress fell.
items.explanation: 'Output was largely maintained, while staff reported lower stress and fewer sick days.'

items.prompt: Why do sceptics doubt the trials can be generalised?
items.answer: The firms that took part were not typical.
items.explanation: 'The companies that volunteered were... disproportionately office-based firms already inclined towards flexible working.'

items.prompt: According to sceptics, what would hospitals face with fewer hours?
items.answer: hiring more staff or reducing service
items.explanation: 'A reduction in hours means either hiring additional staff or reducing the service provided.'

items.prompt: What does 'proponents' mean in the text?
items.explanation: Proponents are people who argue in favour of an idea.

items.prompt: What did the letters reveal about the novelist?
items.answer: She was connected to leading reformers and wrote political pamphlets.
distractors: She was a famous best-selling author.
items.explanation: The letters showed regular contact with reformers and anonymous pamphlets.

items.prompt: Why, according to scholars, was she marginal in literary history?
items.answer: Conventions discouraged women from publishing political work under their names.
distractors: Her writing was of poor quality.
items.explanation: Her status 'owes less to the quality of her work than to the conventions of the period'.

items.prompt: What broader effect has the discovery had?
items.answer: a reassessment of whose voices were preserved
distractors: a new novel about her life
items.explanation: 'The discovery has prompted a broader reassessment of which voices were preserved, and why.'

items.prompt: What were expectations when the trunk was donated?
distractors: Scholars had been searching for it.
items.explanation: 'Few expected it to attract much attention.'

items.prompt: Which phrase best describes the tone of the nudge text?
items.answer: balanced, presenting arguments for and against
items.explanation: The text gives advocates' and critics' views.

items.prompt: ___ to the public in 1759, the British Museum was the first national public museum.
items.explanation: A past participle clause with passive meaning: it was opened.

items.prompt: All things ___, the event was a success.
items.explanation: 'All things considered' is a fixed participle phrase.

items.prompt: The longer the negotiations drag on, the ___ likely a deal becomes.
items.explanation: 'The + comparative..., the less likely...'.

items.prompt: Such ___ the demand that tickets sold out in minutes.
items.explanation: 'Such was the demand that...' (inversion with 'such').

items.prompt: She left the company, ___ surprised everyone.
items.explanation: 'Which' can refer to a whole previous clause.

items.prompt: Were you ___ the position, when could you start?
items.explanation: 'Were + subject + to be + past participle' for a hypothetical passive.

items.prompt: He must have been exhausted, ___ worked for 20 hours straight.
items.explanation: A perfect participle clause gives the reason.

items.prompt: I'll lend you my car on condition ___ you return it by six.
items.explanation: 'On condition that' + clause.

items.prompt: Only after the contract had been signed ___ the hidden costs.
items.explanation: 'Only after...' at the start causes inversion.

items.prompt: The museum is open to the public, ___ on Christmas Day.
items.explanation: 'Except on Christmas Day'.

items.prompt: Far ___ it from me to criticise, but your essay is rather long.
items.explanation: The fixed phrase 'Far be it from me to...' uses the subjunctive.

items.prompt: What matters ___ not how much you earn but how you live.
items.explanation: In this pseudo-cleft, the subject 'What matters' takes 'is'.

items.prompt: At no time ___ aware that the meeting had been recorded.
items.explanation: 'At no time' at the start causes inversion.

items.prompt: The company was forced to ___ its losses and close the factory.
items.explanation: 'Cut your losses' = stop before losing more.

items.prompt: Her performance was nothing ___ of extraordinary.
items.explanation: 'Nothing short of' = really, truly.

items.prompt: The proposal was ___ in principle but rejected in practice.
items.explanation: Something can be welcomed in principle.

items.prompt: He has a ___ interest in the outcome, since he owns shares in the company.
items.explanation: A vested interest = a personal reason for wanting something.

items.prompt: The government is ___ pressure to cut fuel prices.
items.explanation: 'Under pressure' to do something.

items.prompt: The new evidence ___ doubt on his story.
items.explanation: 'Cast doubt on' = make less certain.

items.prompt: The rumours turned out to be completely ___.
items.explanation: Unfounded = not based on facts.

items.prompt: Her career has gone from ___ to strength.
items.explanation: 'Go from strength to strength' = become more successful.

items.prompt: The two leaders held ___ talks on trade.
items.explanation: Bilateral talks involve two countries.

items.prompt: The figures are only a ___ estimate.
items.explanation: A rough estimate is approximate.

items.prompt: She was ___ praised for her handling of the crisis.
items.explanation: 'Widely praised' = praised by many people.

items.prompt: The firm had to ___ its belt after losing the contract.
items.explanation: 'Tighten your belt' = spend less money.

items.prompt: The museum's director ___ down after the scandal.
items.explanation: 'Step down' = resign from a position.

items.prompt: Were it ___ to emerge that the data had been falsified, the consequences would be grave.
items.explanation: 'Were it ever to emerge...' is a formal inverted conditional.

items.prompt: No sooner had the ink dried on the treaty ___ hostilities resumed.
items.explanation: The fixed pattern is 'No sooner had... than'.

items.prompt: ___ though his reasoning may be, the conclusion does not follow.
items.explanation: 'Adjective + though + subject + may be' is a concessive structure.

items.prompt: The committee recommended that the funding ___ withdrawn forthwith.
items.explanation: Mandative subjunctive: base form 'be'.

items.prompt: It is not so much the cost ___ the principle that concerns me.
items.explanation: 'Not so much X as Y'.

items.prompt: Little did the investors suspect the extent ___ which the figures had been manipulated.
items.explanation: 'The extent to which'.

items.prompt: ___ the attention the case has received, a public inquiry seems inevitable.
items.explanation: 'Given' = taking into account.

items.prompt: The report was ___ a whitewash than an investigation.
items.explanation: 'More a whitewash than an investigation'.

items.prompt: Come what ___, we will meet the deadline.
items.explanation: 'Come what may' is a fixed subjunctive expression.

items.prompt: So ___ did the speaker convey her argument that even sceptics were persuaded.
items.explanation: 'So + adverb + did + subject' with inversion.

items.prompt: Were the company ___ by a larger rival, jobs would almost certainly be lost.
items.explanation: Formal hypothetical passive: 'Were + subject + to be + past participle'.

items.prompt: Had it not ___ for the intervention of a passer-by, the fire would have spread.
items.explanation: 'Had it not been for...'.

items.prompt: She is ___ but a reliable witness; her account has changed three times.
items.explanation: 'Anything but' = not at all.

items.prompt: The minister, ___ to have been briefed in advance, denied all knowledge.
items.explanation: A reduced passive relative clause: who was alleged.

items.prompt: There is no denying ___ the policy has had unintended effects.
items.explanation: 'There is no denying that...'.

items.prompt: It was her persistence, ___ her talent, that secured the contract.
items.explanation: 'Rather than' contrasts two noun phrases.

items.prompt: ___ as it may seem, the theory has considerable empirical support.
items.explanation: 'Adjective + as + it may seem' expresses concession.

items.prompt: The suggestion that he ___ resign was met with derision.
items.explanation: 'Suggestion that + should + verb' (or subjunctive).

items.prompt: Only in retrospect ___ the significance of that meeting.
items.explanation: 'Only in retrospect' at the start triggers inversion.

items.prompt: By no ___ is this a definitive account of the period.
items.explanation: 'By no means' = not at all; it causes inversion.

items.prompt: The firm cannot be held liable, ___ the contract was signed under duress.
items.explanation: 'Unless' = except if.

items.prompt: He spoke slowly ___ he be misunderstood.
items.explanation: 'Lest' + (should) + verb = in order to avoid.

items.prompt: Much ___ the critics disliked it, the play ran for three years.
items.explanation: 'Much as' = although very much.

items.prompt: The reforms, ___ well-intentioned, have proved counterproductive.
items.explanation: 'However + adjective' in a concessive phrase.

items.prompt: It is high time measures ___ to protect the coastline.
items.explanation: 'It is high time + past simple (passive)'.

items.prompt: ___ to say, the plan was abandoned within a month.
items.explanation: 'Needless to say' = obviously.

items.prompt: The building, ___ façade dates from 1720, is largely modern inside.
items.explanation: 'Whose' for possession by a thing.

items.prompt: Not a single objection ___ during the consultation.
items.explanation: Passive past simple.

items.prompt: ___ his reservations, he signed the agreement.
items.explanation: 'Notwithstanding' is a formal preposition meaning despite.

items.prompt: The proposal, ___ ambitious, is unlikely to secure funding.
items.explanation: 'Albeit' + adjective = although.

items.prompt: So ___ the damage that the bridge had to be rebuilt.
items.explanation: 'So + adjective + was + subject' (inversion).

items.prompt: Scarcely a day passes ___ some new revelation about the affair.
items.explanation: 'Scarcely a day passes without...'.

items.prompt: I'd sooner they ___ the matter in private.
items.explanation: 'I'd sooner + subject + past simple'.

items.prompt: What little evidence there ___ points to an accident.
items.explanation: 'What little evidence there is' takes a singular verb.

items.prompt: The government's response has been ___ at best.
items.explanation: Lacklustre = lacking energy or effectiveness.

items.prompt: The novel's ending is deliberately ___, leaving readers to draw their own conclusions.
items.explanation: Ambiguous = open to more than one interpretation.

items.prompt: His ___ remarks offended many of those present.
items.explanation: Disparaging = expressing a low opinion.

items.prompt: The witness's testimony was ___ by documentary evidence.
items.explanation: Corroborated = confirmed.

items.prompt: The reforms have been implemented in a ___ fashion, with no overall strategy.
items.explanation: Piecemeal = bit by bit, unsystematically.

items.prompt: She has an ___ ability to remember names.
items.explanation: Uncanny = strange and remarkable.

items.prompt: The minister's explanation was dismissed as ___ special pleading.
items.explanation: 'Mere' + noun = nothing more than.

items.prompt: The company's fortunes have ___ in recent years.
items.explanation: To wane = to decrease gradually.

items.prompt: The proposals were met with ___ silence.
items.explanation: A stony silence is unfriendly and cold.

items.prompt: The author's prose is ___, every word carefully chosen.
items.explanation: Meticulous = showing great attention to detail.

items.prompt: The two theories are not mutually ___.
items.explanation: Mutually exclusive = cannot both be true.

items.prompt: His explanation was so ___ that nobody could follow it.
items.explanation: Convoluted = extremely complex.

items.prompt: The scandal ___ the party's chances at the election.
items.explanation: To scupper = to ruin plans or chances.

items.prompt: The museum's collection is ___ by any standard.
items.explanation: Unrivalled = better than all others.

items.prompt: There was a ___ of applications for the post.
items.explanation: A deluge = a very large number arriving at once.

items.prompt: The film's ___ portrayal of war shocked audiences.
items.explanation: Unflinching = not avoiding unpleasant details.

items.prompt: The negotiations were conducted in a spirit of ___.
items.explanation: Rapprochement = re-establishing friendly relations.

items.prompt: The debate quickly ___ into personal insults.
items.explanation: To degenerate = to become worse.

items.prompt: His argument rests on a number of ___ assumptions.
items.explanation: Questionable = doubtful.

items.prompt: She delivered a ___ critique of the government's policy.
items.explanation: Scathing = severely critical.

items.prompt: The new regulations will be ___ in over the next two years.
items.explanation: 'Phase in' = introduce gradually.

items.prompt: The author ___ the reader with a series of unexpected twists.
items.explanation: To wrong-foot = to put someone at a disadvantage by surprise.

items.prompt: The committee's findings were ___ in their condemnation.
items.explanation: Unequivocal = completely clear, without doubt.

items.prompt: His ___ manner made him popular with colleagues.
items.explanation: Affable = friendly and easy to talk to.

items.prompt: The plan was ___ from the start by a lack of funding.
items.explanation: Hamstrung = severely restricted.

items.prompt: The essay offers a ___ analysis of a complex subject.
items.explanation: Cogent = clear, logical and convincing.

items.prompt: The company was ___ by a series of lawsuits.
items.explanation: Beleaguered = in a very difficult situation.

items.prompt: The novel has been ___ as the finest of its generation.
items.explanation: Lauded = highly praised.

items.prompt: There was a ___ of truth in what he said.
items.explanation: 'A kernel of truth' = a small amount of truth.

items.prompt: The proposal is ___ with practical difficulties.
items.explanation: 'Fraught with' = full of (problems).

items.prompt: She made an ___ attempt to hide her disappointment.
items.explanation: An ill-concealed feeling is badly hidden.

items.prompt: What does the writer say about historical complaints about new media?
items.answer: Each new medium was accused of harming thought.
items.explanation: 'Each new medium... was accused in its day of corrupting the young and fragmenting thought.'

items.prompt: How, according to the writer, are digital platforms different from the novel?
items.answer: Their business models depend on capturing attention.
distractors: They are read by fewer people.
items.explanation: 'The business models of many digital platforms are explicitly predicated on capturing and monetising attention.'

items.prompt: What risk does the writer see in framing the issue as individual willpower?
items.answer: It hides the role of design and places the burden on users.
items.explanation: '...risks obscuring its structural character, and places the burden of resistance on users.'

items.prompt: What is the writer's attitude to present concerns about attention?
items.answer: They are partly valid but often misframed.
distractors: They are entirely new and unprecedented.
items.explanation: 'This is not to dismiss present concerns...' but framing them as willpower is misleading.

items.prompt: What does 'predicated on' mean in the text?
items.explanation: 'Predicated on capturing attention' = based on it.

items.prompt: According to the text, what do monuments often reveal most about?
items.explanation: Monuments 'frequently tell us more about those who commissioned them than about those they depict.'

items.prompt: How does the writer describe moving a statue to a museum?
items.explanation: '...arguably less an act of erasure than of reclassification.'

items.prompt: What does the writer find odd about keeping every monument untouched?
items.answer: It lets one generation's judgements bind all later ones.
items.explanation: '...presupposes that the judgements of one generation should bind all those that follow.'

items.prompt: What 'false dichotomy' does the writer identify?
items.explanation: Debates 'founder on a false dichotomy between preserving history and erasing it.'

items.prompt: What do surveys suggest about trust in expertise?
items.answer: Trust varies: scientists are trusted more than politicians.
distractors: Trust in all experts has collapsed.
items.explanation: 'Confidence in scientists and doctors remains comparatively high, while trust in politicians and journalists is markedly lower.'

items.prompt: What, according to the writer, has eroded?
items.answer: deference to institutions seen as remote or self-serving
items.explanation: 'Less faith in knowledge per se than deference to institutions perceived as remote or self-serving.'

items.prompt: Why might experts who admit uncertainty be trusted more in the long run?
items.answer: They are not exposed when advice changes.
items.explanation: Overconfident experts 'are exposed when... initial advice has to be revised.'

items.prompt: What does 'per se' mean in the text?
items.explanation: 'Faith in knowledge per se' = in knowledge as such.

items.prompt: What was Swift's complaint mentioned in the text?
items.explanation: 'Jonathan Swift lamented the introduction of abbreviations such as 'mob'.'

items.prompt: What is the linguists' main objection, according to the text?
items.explanation: 'Their objection is to the conflation of prestige with correctness.'

items.prompt: What does 'today's solecism is frequently tomorrow's standard usage' mean?
items.answer: What is considered an error now often becomes accepted later.
items.explanation: A solecism is an error; the sentence says errors often become standard.

items.prompt: What is the writer's view of language change?
distractors: It is a sign of decline.
It should be prevented by law.
items.explanation: 'Change is not decay but the normal condition of every living language.'

items.prompt: Why does philanthropy raise questions for democracies?
items.answer: Donors influence public priorities without electoral accountability.
items.explanation: 'It exercises considerable influence over public priorities without being accountable to the electorate.'

items.prompt: What argument do defenders of philanthropy make?
items.answer: Private donors can take risks governments avoid.
items.explanation: 'Private donors can take risks that governments, wary of public criticism, cannot.'

items.prompt: What point do sceptics make about tax relief?
items.answer: The public effectively subsidises decisions it cannot influence.
distractors: Donors don't receive any tax relief.
items.explanation: 'The public effectively subsidises decisions in which it has no say.'

items.prompt: What does the Mercator projection preserve, according to the text?
items.explanation: 'Preserves angles at the expense of area.'

items.prompt: What effect does the Mercator projection have on regions near the poles?
items.answer: They look much larger than they are.
items.explanation: 'Making regions near the poles appear far larger than they are.'

items.prompt: How have cartographers' decisions sometimes been used politically?
items.explanation: Decisions 'have at times been instrumental in asserting territorial claims.'

items.prompt: What does 'belies' mean in the first sentence?
items.explanation: The aura of objectivity belies (disguises) the choices behind maps.

items.prompt: Which choice is NOT mentioned as one cartographers make?
items.answer: the paper the map is printed on
items.explanation: The text mentions inclusion, naming and language.

items.prompt: What does the writer imply about 'reliable'?
items.answer: Commentators once disliked it, though it is now standard.
items.explanation: Later commentators 'deplored 'reliable' as an ugly hybrid', yet it is now normal.

items.prompt: Try ___ they might, the negotiators could not break the deadlock.
items.explanation: 'Try as they might' = however hard they tried.

items.prompt: Be that as it ___, we still need a decision by Friday.
items.explanation: 'Be that as it may' = nevertheless.

items.prompt: It is imperative that the data ___ independently verified.
items.explanation: Mandative subjunctive after 'imperative that'.

items.prompt: Not until the final chapter ___ the narrator's true identity revealed.
items.explanation: 'Not until...' at the start causes inversion: 'is the identity revealed'.

items.prompt: Should the need ___, additional staff will be recruited.
items.explanation: 'Should + subject + base form' = if the need arises.

items.prompt: She has, ___ all accounts, been an exemplary colleague.
items.explanation: 'By all accounts' = according to what everyone says.

items.prompt: The findings are, if anything, ___ than expected.
items.explanation: 'If anything' + comparative suggests the opposite of what might be expected.

items.prompt: Inasmuch ___ the board approved the plan, it shares responsibility.
items.explanation: 'Inasmuch as' = to the extent that.

items.prompt: But ___ his outspoken criticism, he would have been promoted.
items.explanation: 'But for' = if it were not for.

items.prompt: ___ the case may be, the procedure remains the same.
items.explanation: 'Whatever the case may be' = in any case.

items.prompt: The report makes for ___ reading.
items.explanation: 'Make for sobering reading' = cause serious thought.

items.prompt: His rise to power was ___.
items.explanation: Meteoric = very rapid.

items.prompt: The two parties have reached an ___ agreement, pending final approval.
items.explanation: An agreement in principle is agreed generally but not in detail.

items.prompt: The campaign gained ___ after the celebrity endorsement.
items.explanation: Gain traction = become popular or accepted.

items.prompt: The museum's acquisition was ___ by controversy.
items.explanation: Dogged by = continually troubled by.

items.prompt: The author's latest work is a ___ departure from her earlier style.
items.explanation: A marked departure = a noticeable change.

items.prompt: The evidence against him was ___.
items.explanation: Overwhelming = very great in amount or strength.

items.prompt: The proposal was rejected on the ___ that it was too costly.
items.explanation: 'On the grounds that' = because.

items.prompt: She ___ through the report in under an hour.
items.explanation: To plough through = read with effort.

items.prompt: There is a ___ line between persuasion and manipulation.
items.explanation: 'A fine line' = a small difference.

items.prompt: The company's ___ for innovation has made it an industry leader.
items.explanation: A penchant = a strong liking.

items.prompt: The government has been ___ for its handling of the crisis.
items.explanation: Pilloried = strongly criticised in public.

items.prompt: The terms of the agreement are ___ to change without notice.
items.explanation: 'Subject to' = may be affected by.

items.prompt: Her arguments were ___ and well supported.
items.explanation: Incisive = clear and sharp.

items.prompt: The novel is a ___ satire of Victorian society.
items.explanation: A biting satire is sharp and critical.

items.prompt: The investigation uncovered a ___ of corruption.
items.explanation: 'A web of corruption' = a complex network.

items.prompt: They are ___ to agree on anything.
items.explanation: Loath (adjective) = unwilling; loathe (verb) = hate.

items.prompt: The proposal was quietly ___.
items.explanation: Jettisoned = abandoned.

items.prompt: He gave a ___ account of the events, omitting key details.
items.explanation: A selective account includes only some facts.
